- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.7) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce peak overshoots by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to sentiment-driven momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤ -0.3) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward bias — adjust downward only if 2+ consecutive days show negative sentiment.
- For 30-day forecasts, if the last 3–5 days of history show strong mean reversion (e.g., 2–3 consecutive price drops or sentiment dips), reduce forecast volatility and favor smoother, trend-following paths.
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral (±0.3), avoid large swings — model should favor mid-range or slightly upward bias unless recent price action shows clear breakout.
- If forecast consistently overestimates prices after a spike (e.g., +10%+ above true outcome), apply a “cool-down” correction: subtract 2–5% from the next 3–5 forecast points to reflect diminishing momentum.
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment history shows a recent spike followed by a drop, model should anticipate a “reversion-to-mean” correction — reduce forecast peak and add a slight downward bias in the following 5–7 days.
- If sentiment is consistently positive but price action shows no upward momentum (e.g., 3+ days of flat or slightly declining prices), reduce forecast slope — avoid assuming sentiment will drive price higher unless confirmed by price action.
